The range is set by the length of the neck, commonly twenty-seven frets, giving the twelve-note chromatic scale; there are three courses of six strings, four courses of eight, and five courses of ten with an extra course an octave lower to extend the range. Its predecessors can be traced to the pandura and the tambura; early bodies were mostly carved from solid wood, and in Greece a Neapolitan mandolin-style staved back was adopted to bear the steel strings. The three-course form long dominated rebetiko, and after the 1950s the four-course form became popular through Manolis Chiotis, with a first recording in 1956. It reached Ireland around 1965 and gave rise to the Irish bouzouki.

The bouzouki is a plucked instrument of the long-necked lute family common in Greece, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321. It has a round body, a long neck and a fretted fingerboard, is strung with steel and played with a plectrum, and its sharp metallic sound lies lower than the mandolin's. After Greek refugees from Asia Minor brought it to Greece in the early twentieth century it became the core instrument of rebetiko music, and it is now also common in Laïko Greek popular music; its offshoot, the Irish bouzouki, appears in Celtic, English and North American folk music.

琴身共鳴箱以實木慢生木材製成，較佳者包括桑木、杏木、櫻桃木、金合歡木與榆木，胡桃: The body and resonator are made from slow-grown solid woods, the better ones including mulberry, apricot, cherry, acacia and elm, with walnut, plane and chestnut a little inferior. The top is of fir or spruce, spruce preferred, and cut in one piece. The strings are steel. The modern neck uses very dry hard wood, some with a metal adjusting rod inside; the frets are metal, where early instruments used gut or cord. The finish is hand-applied in several coats of natural shellac.
